source.title: Spec: Agent-driven engineering studio (repo fix → M0 walking skeleton → M1 calibration → M2 ESP32 enclosure → M3 mechanism)

labels.name: ready-for-agent
labels.description: Fully specified; an AFK agent can finish it against automated tests

source.body:
## Problem Statement

I have an idea for a physical thing: a holder, a case for a circuit board, a small mechanism. I can measure things with calipers and I own a good 3D printer, but I can't use Fusion 360 or SolidWorks. Learning them takes months, and an idea is useless until it's a part that actually fits.

Today, Magic CAD can rigorously check a part designed by an outside coding agent. But I have to drive Claude Code myself, write briefs by hand, and read gate reports in a developer view. The app can't take my words or a click on the model and turn them into a design change.

It also can't handle anything with more than one part: no screws, no purchased boards, no parts list, no exploded view, no assembly instructions, no motion. And it doesn't learn from my real prints. The printer settings in the project are still placeholders, so the first real print of anything is a guess.

## Solution

Magic CAD becomes an agent-driven engineering studio that runs on my own machine. I describe what I want in plain language, add measurements, or click and outline areas on the 3D model, and a small team of agents does the work:

- A **lead agent** writes the brief card.
- A **designer agent** writes parametric build123d code until the harness gates pass.
- A **reviewer agent** independently scores the design.

I watch the work live and accept or reject each proposed change. Every accepted change is a version I can roll back to.

The app has three modes over the same project:
- **Make** is the guided Ask → Make → Prove → Shelf flow.
- **Studio** is the 3D workspace with selection tools, exploded view, motion, assembly playback and the agent chat.
- **Mission Control** is expert mode, one tap away: brief cards, gate reports, evals, the library and the code.

Multi-part products are described by an **assembly** that combines my printed parts, standard hardware and purchased components. From the assembly, the app derives the parts list, exploded view, assembly order, assembly instructions and, later, motion.

Every claim the app makes is labelled with its evidence tier:
- **computed**
- **slicer-checked**
- **needs a physical test**

When I print something and record the result, the app proposes calibration updates for my Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2, with the evidence shown. It only applies them when I approve. It also records written lessons the agents read next time, and turns finished projects into regression evals, so the agents' modelling improves on my machine.

The work is delivered in milestones:
- A **repo fix**.
- **M0, a walking skeleton:** chat → agent edits a design → gates stream → Studio updates → version saved.
- **M1, calibration.**
- **M2, an ESP32 electronics enclosure:** the first complete idea-to-printed-product run.
- **M3, a simple mechanism with motion.**

The bike-pump holder was the first proof. An engine assembly stays the long-term north star, not a milestone here.

## User Stories

### Describing and briefing
1. As a maker, I want to describe the thing I need in plain language, so that I don't need to learn CAD to start a design.
2. As a maker, I want to add measurements I took with calipers to my description, so that the design fits my real objects.
3. As a maker, I want the lead agent to ask me at most a handful of clarifying questions before it designs, so that I'm not interrogated but the result isn't a guess.
4. As a maker, I want each clarifying question to come with a sensible recommended answer, so that I can accept it in one word.
5. As a maker, I want the lead agent to write the brief card for me in the background, so that the design has hard, checkable requirements without me writing YAML.
6. As an expert user, I want to open and edit the brief card in Mission Control, so that I can pin exact dimensions, ranges or materials.
7. As a maker, I want the agent to tell me which of my requirements it could not turn into a measurable check, so that I know what is untested.

### Agents at work
8. As a maker, I want the designer agent to write and fix the parametric design until all harness gates pass, so that I only see designs that passed the automated checks.
9. As a maker, I want an independent reviewer agent to score each passing design against the brief, so that "passed the gates" isn't mistaken for "good design".
10. As a maker, I want to see the reviewer's named problems and required fixes, so that I understand why a design was sent back.
11. As a maker, I want to see the agents' plan, which file they're editing, and each gate passing or failing as it happens, so that a multi-minute design loop doesn't feel like a black box.
12. As a maker, I want to interrupt or redirect the agents mid-run, so that I can stop wasted work when I see it going wrong.
13. As a maker, I want, as a stretch goal, to see the latest successfully built geometry appear as a translucent "not yet checked" model while agents work, so that I can watch my design take shape.
14. As a maker, I want each finished run to end with a clear verdict split into computed, slicer-checked and needs-physical-test, so that I know exactly how much to trust it.
15. As a maker, I want the app to use my existing Claude Code login, so that I don't have to manage an API key.
16. As a maker, I want the app never to store my Claude credentials itself, so that my account stays safe.
17. As a maker, I want to see how long a design session took and what it cost in usage where available, so that agent work is predictable.

### Changing a design
18. As a maker, I want to ask for a change in plain language ("make the wall 1 mm thicker, move the USB hole up"), so that I can iterate without touching code.
19. As a maker, I want each proposed change shown as a before/after preview with the exact parameters that change, so that I approve changes knowingly.
20. As a maker, I want the gates to re-run automatically after I accept a change, so that every version I keep is checked.
21. As a maker, I want the verdict change from the last version to be shown plainly, so that I notice when a change broke something.
22. As a maker, I want every accepted change saved as a version on a timeline, so that I can roll back any time.
23. As a maker, I want to roll back to an earlier version in one action, so that experiments are safe.
24. As a maker, I want to edit exposed parameters directly with controls, so that small numeric tweaks don't need a conversation.
25. As an expert user, I want to read the generated design code, so that I can verify or learn from what the agent did.

### Selecting on the model
26. As a maker, I want to click a whole part to select it, so that I can talk about "this part".
27. As a maker, I want to click a single surface to select it, so that I can ask for a change to exactly that face.
28. As a maker, I want to draw a freehand outline around any area on screen, so that I can select a region that isn't a single face or part.
29. As a maker, I want to drop a note pin on the model with a short comment ("this is too thin"), so that my feedback is attached to the right place.
30. As a maker, I want to measure the distance or angle between two picks, so that I can check a dimension myself.
31. As a maker, I want whatever I select to be passed to the agent with its feature name, measured dimensions and the picked points, so that the agent knows exactly what I mean.
32. As a maker, I want selected areas to be named the way the design names them (e.g. "USB cutout"), so that the conversation uses meaningful words, not coordinates.

### Studio workspace
33. As a maker, I want to orbit, pan and zoom the model in a crisp 3D workspace, so that I can inspect it from any angle.
34. As a maker, I want an exploded view I can scrub with a slider, so that I can see every part of an assembly separately.
35. As a maker, I want to see the parts move along their joints for a mechanism, so that I can check it moves the way I expect.
36. As a maker, I want to be warned when moving parts collide anywhere in their range of motion, so that a mechanism that jams is caught before printing.
37. As a maker, I want a clear distinction between "animation" and a physically validated test, so that motion playback isn't mistaken for proof.
38. As a maker, I want the assembly tree listing every part, hardware item and purchased component, so that I can find and isolate anything.
39. As a maker, I want to hide, isolate or ghost individual parts, so that I can see inside an assembly.

### Three modes, one project
40. As a maker, I want Make, Studio and Mission Control to always show the same project and version, so that switching modes never loses my place.
41. As a maker, I want my current selection to stay selected when I switch modes, so that I can jump to engineering details about the same thing.
42. As a maker, I want Make to walk me through Ask → Make → Prove → Shelf, so that the simple path stays simple.
43. As an expert user, I want Mission Control to show brief cards, gate reports, evals, the library and reports for the open project, so that engineering detail is one tap away.
44. As a maker, I want every finished part or product saved to my Shelf with its proof and version history, so that I can remake or remix it later.

### Projects and versions
45. As a maker, I want each project stored as a plain folder on my computer, so that I own my files.
46. As a maker, I want the version history to be stored without me ever seeing git, so that versioning is simple.
47. As a maker, I want to open an existing project folder and continue where I left off, so that work survives restarts.

### Assemblies, hardware and purchased parts
48. As a maker, I want my product to be made of several printed parts plus screws, inserts and bought components, so that I can build real products, not single blocks.
49. As a maker, I want the agents to choose suitable standard hardware (e.g. M2.5 screws and heat-set inserts) from the library, so that I don't have to know fastener standards.
50. As a maker, I want to pick a purchased component (e.g. an ESP32-DevKitC) from a catalogue, so that my enclosure is designed around the real board.
51. As a maker, I want each catalogue component to show its key dimensions, keep-out space, mounting points and a source link, so that I can trust what the design is built around.
52. As a maker, I want each catalogue dimension labelled as checked against a datasheet, checked against a real part, or unverified, so that I know which numbers are solid.
53. As a maker, I want to add my own component by entering caliper measurements, so that I'm not limited to the catalogue.
54. As a maker, I want my own components labelled "user-measured", so that their reliability is clear.
55. As a maker, I want an assembly gate that checks for parts colliding and for fasteners actually fitting their holes and bosses, so that the assembly can physically go together.

### Parts list, outputs and instructions
56. As a maker, I want a parts list generated from the assembly, so that I know every printed part, screw and component I need.
57. As a maker, I want the parts list to always match the assembly, so that it can never go out of date.
58. As a maker, I want 3MF and STEP files exported for passing designs, so that I can print the parts and use them in other tools.
59. As a maker, I want production exports offered only when the required gates pass, so that I never print an unchecked design by accident.
60. As a maker, I want to choose the style of assembly instructions, so that they suit how experienced I am.
61. As a maker, I want illustrated step-by-step instructions by default, each with a picture of that stage, hardware callouts and the tool needed, so that I can assemble without guessing.
62. As a maker, I want to play the assembly as an animation in Studio, so that I can see how it goes together.
63. As an experienced maker, I want a compact checklist style, so that I don't wade through pictures I don't need.
64. As a maker, I want to export instructions as a standalone HTML page or PDF, so that I can use them at my workbench.
65. As a maker, I want all instruction styles generated from the same assembly, so that they never disagree.

### Printer, slicer and calibration
66. As a maker, I want my Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 set up as a printer profile, so that the build volume and nozzle are real, not placeholders.
67. As a maker, I want separate profiles for PLA and PETG, so that clearances match the material I'm printing.
68. As a maker, I want to print a small calibration test piece on first run, so that fits, holes and overhang limits come from my printer, not guesses.
69. As a maker, I want every design sliced with ElegooSlicer on my machine, so that print time, material and supports are checked against a real slicer.
70. As a maker, I want slicer results to upgrade a claim to "slicer-checked", so that the evidence tier reflects reality.
71. As a maker, I want the app never to send a print job itself, so that physical actions stay under my control.

### Learning from real prints
72. As a maker, I want to rate each print's fits (perfect, too tight, too loose, broke) in a few taps, so that recording results is quick.
73. As a maker, I want to optionally add caliper measurements of named features and a photo, so that the evidence is richer when I have time.
74. As a maker, I want the app to propose calibration changes with the supporting evidence ("3 prints, all too tight → +0.10 mm sliding fit"), so that I understand why numbers change.
75. As a maker, I want calibration changes applied only after I approve them, so that one bad print can't silently skew everything.
76. As a maker, I want a recorded physical result to upgrade the matching claims to "physically tested", so that my verdicts reflect reality.
77. As a maker, I want failures turned into written lessons the agents read on every future design, so that the same mistake isn't repeated.
78. As a maker, I want each finished project to become a regression eval, so that a later improvement can't quietly break an earlier design.
79. As a maker, I want all of this learning kept on my machine, so that my data stays private.

### Milestone demos
80. As Addison, I want a walking skeleton (M0) where I type a change in the new app, Claude Code edits the wall bracket, gates stream back, Studio updates, and a version is saved, so that every layer is proven connected before features pile on.
81. As Addison, I want M1 to deliver the printer profile, calibration piece, slicer check, print-result capture and approved calibration updates, so that M2's print uses calibrated numbers.
82. As Addison, I want M2 to take "a wall-mountable case for an ESP32-DevKitC with the USB port reachable" through to an enclosure with base, lid, board, M2.5 screws and inserts, so that the whole idea-to-product loop is proven once.
83. As Addison, I want M2's steps up to and including a selection-driven edit to work with no manual fixes, so that the demo proves the product, not my intervention.
84. As Addison, I want M2 to end with one real print and a recorded fit, so that the milestone is closed by reality.
85. As Addison, I want M3 to add joints, motion playback and clearance checks across motion for a simple mechanism, so that the product grows toward mechanisms safely.

### Developer and agent loop
86. As Addison, I want the existing harness, gates and tests kept and extended, not rewritten, so that proven checks aren't lost.
87. As Addison, I want the repo-fix work done first (missing eval briefs restored, the UI test's missing model files, planter_pot redesigned to pass the overhang gate without weakening it, Linux paths in the MCP setup guide), so that the agent loop starts from a trustworthy green baseline.
88. As Addison, I want each ticket worked on its own branch with its own pull request, so that I review everything before it merges.
89. As Addison, I want nothing merged without me, so that I stay in control of the codebase.
90. As Addison, I want the agent-runtime adapter designed so Codex can be added later, so that I'm not locked into one provider.
91. As Addison, I want the agent layer kept separate from the local CAD engine, so that a hosted version is possible later without a rewrite.

## Implementation Decisions

**Product and scope**
- Target user: FDM makers without CAD skills. Engineering detail is hidden by default and one tap away.
- Manufacturing process: FDM printing only, plus STEP export. Each part records its manufacturing process so other processes can be added later.
- Source of truth: every printed part is a parametric build123d design following the existing design contract: a `PARAMS` table with default, minimum and maximum values, a `build(**params)` function, and no hard-coded literals. Users change designs through conversation and exposed parameters, and code is readable on request.
- The bike-pump holder was the first proof. Milestones are the repo fix, M0, M1, M2 and M3. An engine assembly is the north star, not a milestone.

**Architecture**
- **Build on the existing repo.** The harness (`magic.py` and its gates), proof app, Studio, Mission Control, MCP server and library are extended, not replaced. Nothing is deleted until its replacement passes the same tests. This spec extends `PRODUCT_VISION_UX_SPEC.md`.
- **Local-first.** CAD work runs on the user's computer, with no account. The agent layer sits behind an interface so a hosted backend could replace it later.
- **Two halves:**
  - The **Python engine**: the harness, gates, assembly model, catalogue, slicer, calibration, project storage and instructions generator. It is exposed through one local HTTP API.
  - The **TypeScript app**, built with React and react-three-fiber. It has three modes over one shared project state.

  The existing plain-JS Studio and Mission Control are ported piece by piece, keeping the Impeccable design bar and the slop bans in the project's UI design docs.
- **Engine API (the main seam).** "Project folder in → verdict + artifacts out". It covers:
  - run gates on a project or version
  - stream gate and agent events
  - list and roll back versions
  - list catalogue and library items
  - slice a part
  - record a print result
  - propose and apply calibration
  - generate the parts list and instructions

  The existing CLI stays as a thin wrapper over the same functions.
- **Agent runtime adapter.** A narrow interface: start a session with a project, brief and selection context; stream events; interrupt; resume.
  - The first and only implementation drives the locally installed Claude Code headless (Claude Agent SDK or `claude -p`) using the user's existing Claude Code login.
  - The app never stores tokens.
  - A Codex implementation can be added later behind the same interface.
  - The agents use the existing project skills and the build123d and magic-cad MCP servers.
- **Agent roles:**
  - **Lead:** talks to the user, asks at most about 5 clarifying questions, each with a recommendation, writes the brief card.
  - **Designer:** writes and fixes the design code until the gates pass.
  - **Reviewer:** runs the existing magic-cad-reviewer critique independently and has no say in authoring.

  Add more roles only when a milestone needs them.
- **Projects and versions.**
  - Each project is a folder holding its brief card(s), part designs, an assembly file, gate reports and generated outputs.
  - A git repository inside the project folder stores versions. Every accepted change is a commit.
  - The UI shows a version timeline, never git.
  - Rollback restores a version and re-runs the gates.
- **Change proposals.** An agent change is held as a proposal showing the parameter changes (old → new) and a before/after preview. Accepting it commits a version and re-runs the gates. The verdict change is reported against the previous version.
- **Live progress.** Agent and gate events stream to the app. The user can interrupt at any time. A stretch goal is that whenever the design code runs successfully, Studio shows that latest geometry as translucent "not yet checked" until every gate passes.

**Assembly model**
- A new assembly file per multi-part project declares:
  - printed part instances, each referencing its own parametric design
  - standard hardware instances from the library
  - purchased components from the catalogue
  - placements and connections expressed with build123d joints
- Derived from the assembly, never written by hand: the parts list, exploded view offsets, assembly order, assembly instructions and (M3) motion ranges.
- A new **assembly gate**, alongside the existing five, checks:
  - collisions between parts
  - fastener fit: screw length against hole depth plus insert, and clearance-hole size from the fits table
  - every parts-list and instruction entry referring to exactly one assembly instance, generalising the existing assembly demo's validation

  In M3 it extends to clearance across the whole range of motion.

**Catalogue and library**
- The purchased-component catalogue is curated and local. Each entry has:
  - key dimensions
  - keep-out geometry (the envelope including connectors and access clearances)
  - mounting points
  - a source link
  - a per-dimension provenance label: datasheet-verified, part-verified, unverified, or user-measured

  It has no prices and no live sourcing.
- The first entry is the ESP32-DevKitC. The library gains M2.5 screws and M2.5 heat-set inserts. Existing entries written from memory are relabelled unverified until checked.
- Users can add components from caliper measurements, labelled user-measured.

**Selection**
- The Studio toolbar has five tools: part, surface, freehand outline (lasso), note pin, and measure (distance or angle).
- Every tool feeds one selection object passed to the agent. It contains:
  - part instance name
  - feature name(s)
  - measured dimensions
  - picked or enclosed points in model coordinates
  - the user's note
- The harness exports a **face → feature-name map** alongside each mesh, from labels that designs assign to named features. When a face has no label, it falls back to a geometric description (position, normal, area).
- Edge and point selection are later.

**Evidence tiers and verdicts**
- Every claim carries one of three tiers:
  - **computed:** gates, fits, interference, printability analysis
  - **slicer-checked:** ElegooSlicer time, material, supports
  - **physically tested:** a recorded print result
- Claims that need a test and haven't had one are shown as "needs physical test". A recorded result upgrades the matching claims. No UI copy may imply physical confidence without that evidence.
- Production exports (3MF, STEP) are offered only when the required gates pass. Drafts and failed checks are clearly labelled.

**Printer, slicer and calibration**
- The printer profile is the Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 (256 × 256 × 256 mm build volume, 0.4 mm nozzle), with PLA and PETG material profiles and single colour only. The profile replaces the placeholder printer and clearance values in the project guidelines. The bed-fit gate reads the profile.
- The slicer is the local ElegooSlicer command-line tool (it can slice, arrange, orient and export 3MF), using its built-in Centauri Carbon 2 machine profiles. The app never sends a print job.
- The calibration piece is a small coupon with sliding, press and print-in-place fit gaps, test holes and an overhang ladder. It is part of first-run setup (M1).
- Print results:
  - each joint or fit gets a quick rating, as the proof app does today
  - optional caliper measurements of named features and an optional photo can be added
  - results are appended to the existing outcomes log
- Calibration proposals: the engine proposes per-fit-type adjustments with their evidence count and history. They are applied only on user approval. A single print can suggest a change but never applies it automatically.

**Learning (local only, no fine-tuning)**
- The calibration profile improves from print evidence (above).
- **Lessons:** failures and review findings become written rules in project knowledge the agents read every session, extending the kernel-pitfalls and reviewer skills.
- **Regression evals:** each finished project's brief card and design join the eval corpus.

**Assembly instructions**
- Instructions are generated from the assembly order and joints. Each step has an automatically rendered image of that stage, hardware callouts (e.g. "2× M2.5×8 socket head"), and the tool needed.
- Three styles in M2: illustrated steps (the default), animated playback in Studio, and a compact checklist. They export as a standalone HTML page or PDF. A wordless style is later.

**Development process**
- Tickets are GitHub issues on AddisonJPratt/CAD-ADE, sub-issues of this spec, labelled `ready-for-agent` (finishable by an agent alone against automated tests) or `ready-for-human` (needs review or a demo).
- One branch and pull request per ticket. Nothing merges without Addison.
- Agents never send print jobs or apply calibration without approval.

## Testing Decisions

- **What a good test is:** it exercises external behaviour through a public seam and asserts on outcomes a user would care about: verdicts, measured dimensions, exported files, the parts list, instruction steps, versions. It never asserts on private functions or internal structure. Negative controls (designs that must fail a gate) are as important as passing cases.
- **Seam 1, the engine:** "project folder in → verdict + artifacts out", via the engine API, with the CLI as a thin wrapper. Everything below is tested here:
  - every engine feature: assembly gate, catalogue, face → feature map, parts list, instructions, slicer wrapper, print-result capture, calibration proposals, versions and rollback
  - fixture project folders, both passing and deliberately broken
- **Seam 2, the app:** Playwright end-to-end tests of the TypeScript app against the real engine API, with the agent runtime replaced by a **scripted fake agent** that emits a recorded event stream and file edits. They cover chat → proposal → accept → gates → Studio update → version timeline, selection tools producing the right selection payload, mode switching that keeps project and selection, exploded view and instruction playback.
- **Real agent runs** are not part of the normal test suite. They live in the eval suite (the existing eval runner and corpus) because they are slow, cost usage, and are nondeterministic.
- **Slicer tests** run the real ElegooSlicer command-line tool where it is installed, and are skipped with a clear message where it isn't.
- **Prior art in the repo:**
  - the harness negative-control fixtures (crash, hang, hard-coded literal, dead parameter, overlap, oversize, wrong dimension, flat ceiling) in the main test runner
  - the eval-corpus tests
  - the MCP server test with a real stdio client session
  - the holder fit and proof app tests, including desktop readiness
  - the assembly demo test (static screw/clip interference plus drift detection), which is the model for the assembly gate
  - the Studio core unit tests run with Node's test runner
- **Baseline:** the repo-fix ticket must make every existing suite green on a fresh clone (including the Studio framing test that needs real model files) before feature tickets start.

## Out of Scope

- Manufacturing processes other than FDM printing (CNC, laser/sheet metal, injection moulding, PCB fabrication), beyond STEP export.
- Multi-colour or multi-material printing, including the Centauri Carbon 2 Combo's colour unit.
- Sending print jobs to the printer.
- Prices, live supplier lookups, ordering or sourcing of hardware and components.
- A hosted or cloud version, user accounts, and sharing calibration or lessons between users.
- API-key authentication and any third-party commercial use of Claude subscription logins. Required before selling to others; see Further Notes.
- A Codex implementation of the agent runtime. Only the interface is designed for it.
- Fine-tuning or training models.
- Edge and point selection tools and drawing on the model.
- The wordless picture-only instruction style.
- Physics simulation, load or strength analysis beyond existing lightweight estimates, and anything that claims physical validation without a recorded print.
- Engine-like assemblies; the engine stays the north star.
- Items from the existing vision doc not decided here: camera or photo capture of the user's world, AR "preview in place", and multiple design variants per request.
- Distributing the desktop app (bundled Python runtime, signing, installer). The Tauri shell remains a development shell.

## Further Notes

- **Claude login policy.** In February 2026 Anthropic's docs stated that Free, Pro and Max subscription logins are intended only for Claude Code and Claude.ai, and that third-party products built on the Agent SDK should use API keys. Anthropic staff said local development and `claude -p` are encouraged. Using Addison's own Claude Code login locally is the decision for now. Before anyone else pays for or uses the app, add API-key auth or re-check Anthropic's current terms.
- **Principles carried over from the vision doc:**
  - agents propose; checks and evidence establish what is known
  - never weaken a gate to make a design pass
  - a gate pass is not a design verdict
  - reality is the source of truth
  - expert mode is one tap away
  - original designs only; decline weapon or firearm components
- **The `planter_pot` decision.** Keep the 15% overhang gate and redesign the pot to pass. Do not relax the gate.
- **Slicer choice.** ElegooSlicer is used rather than OrcaSlicer. The "Orca" app installed on Addison's Mac is unrelated to OrcaSlicer.
- **gh version.** This machine has `gh` 2.88, older than the 2.94 needed for the sub-issue and blocked-by shortcuts. Use the `gh api` fallbacks documented in the project's agent docs when linking tickets.
- **Tracker setup.** The ticket tracker and labels were configured on 2026-11-04 on branch `chore/setup-matt-pocock-skills`, which has not been merged yet.
